problems.problem: Mars orbits the Sun at an average distance of $2.28 \times 10^{11}$ m and has a radius of $3.39 \times 10^{6}$ m. The Sun has a luminosity of $3.828 \times 10^{26}$ W. How much solar energy falls on the surface of Mars each second? Ignore any effects of Mars' thin atmosphere.

Suppose that at some time in the very recent past all the hydrogen and helium in the universe had been instantly fused into iron in stars, and the released energy thermalized into black body radiation.

Consider: baryon density $\rho_b = 4.2 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{3}}$, about 75% hydrogen (=1 baryon) by mass and 25% helium (=4 baryons) by mass.

Note that the binding energy per nucleon of ${}^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ is 8.8 MeV and that of ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ is 7.1 MeV.)

a) What is the current temperature of this black body radiation? (2 points)

b) Determine what wavelength the blackbody spectrum would peak at. What region of the electromagnetic spectrum would this be in? (1 point)

His 70 kg massive body is now separated 1 m from the space station and at rest relative to it. Luckily, he has a strong flashlight in his pocket that radiates light with a power of 10 W! (5 points) Cepheid variable stars are pulsating stars whose absolute magnitude $M$ changes as the stars swell larger and smaller in a regular pattern with period $P$. Data from many observations have shown that there is a relationship between $M$ and $P$ on the particular form $M = A \cdot \log_{10}(P/\mathrm{days}) + B$ with constant $A$ and $B$. In other words, if we can observe the period, the absolute magnitude is known, so we call these stars standard candles: astronomical objects with known luminosity. This makes cepheids excellent targets for distance measurements!

a) (3 points) Seven cepheid variables have been observed pulsating with the average absolute magnitudes and periods below.

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Star} & \text{A} & \text{B} & \text{C} & \text{D} & \text{E} & \text{F} & \text{G} \\ \hline P/\text{days} & 6.75 & 4.24 & 4.48 & 16.41 & 10.14 & 1.95 & 8.00 \\ \hline M & -3.64 & -3.04 & -3.09 & -4.69 & -4.10 & -1.99 & -3.80 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Use a piece of gridded paper. Plot and fit the data points to the relation above with a straight line in a (x,y)-diagram, and find the coefficients $A$ and $B$. Show your calculations, label your axes and handle units properly to score all points.

b) (2 points) Another cepheid is observed with the apparent magnitude $m = 5.5$ (not to be confused with its absolute magnitude $M$) and the pulsation pattern below. How many parsecs away is this star?

problems.problem:
(6 points) A black hole with mass $M$ radiates energy from its event horizon through Hawking radiation. This radiation has a black body spectrum with temperature $T = \hbar c^3/8\pi G M k$, where $\hbar = h/2\pi$ is the reduced Planck constant, $G$ is the gravitational constant and $k$ is the Boltzmann constant. Thus, the same physical laws as for other black bodies apply (e.g. stars). This means that even a black hole, from which "nothing can escape", leaks energy and eventually evaporates!

a) (2 points) Show that the luminosity radiated by the black hole can be written $L = L_\odot \cdot \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{-2}$, where $M_\odot$ is the Sun's mass and $L_\odot$ is the luminosity radiated by a black hole with the Sun's mass. Hint: just calculate with proportionalities like $T \propto M^{-1}$; you do not have to express $L_\odot$ explicitly!

b) (2 points) Assume the black hole radiates with constant luminosity. Show that the lifetime of a black hole (the time it takes for it to evaporate) can be written $t = t_\odot \cdot \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{3}$, where $t_\odot$ is the lifetime of a solar mass black hole. Also express $t_\odot$ in terms of $L_\odot$, $M_\odot$ and physical constants.

c) (2 points) It is possible to calculate that $t_\odot \approx 10^{67}$ years (you actually have all needed numbers, but we will just give it for simplicity). Today, scientists are eagerly hoping to observe primordial black holes that explode as they reach the end of the evaporation process. Why is there a maximum mass of primordial black holes we can observe today? What is the value of this mass?

problems.problem:
(10 points) Not all stars that exhibit interesting properties have been assigned a common name. One such star is $\eta$Car, a seemingly unremarkable star in the southern constellation Carina. The plot under this text shows an incredible increase in apparent brightness this star exhibited in the mid-1800s, termed "The Great Eruption". At the peak, $\eta$Car became the second brightest star in the sky, just under Sirius. Its mass is estimated to be around $100 M_\odot$ and it is located approximately 7500ly away from us.

a) (1 point) Sir Arthur S. Eddington defined an upper limit for the luminosity of a star that is in hydrostatic equilibrium. This Eddington limit can be described by the expression $L_{Edd} = 3.2 \cdot 10^4 \cdot \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right) L_\odot$, so if a star with mass $M$ surpasses this luminosity, theory would state that its radiation pressure has become greater than the gravitational force holding the star together. What would be the result of the radiation pressure overcoming gravity?

b) (1 point) Did $\eta$Car ever cross this theoretical limit during its "Great Eruption"? How about during the second "Lesser Eruption" around 1890? Comment on these findings in the context of your answer in a). Take the Sun's absolute magnitude to be 4.83

c) (7 points) In the 1990s, both amateur and professional observations started noting a steady brightening in $\eta$Car's magnitude, hypothesised to be due to dissipation of a dust cloud located in front of the star. This brightening has continued on for several decades at approximately the same rate. You are provided with apparent magnitude data of $\eta$Car between the years 2020-2025¹. Use the provided millimetre paper to plot these points accordingly, and draw a best fit line through them.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Year} & \text{Apparent Magnitude [mag]} \\ \hline 2020 & 4.27 \\ \hline 2021 & 4.16 \\ \hline 2022 & 4.04 \\ \hline 2023 & 3.93 \\ \hline 2024 & 3.82 \\ \hline 2025 & 3.70 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

¹ Data taken from https://www.aavso.org/ and https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.00531

d) (1 point) $\eta$Car is surrounded by a nebula called Homunculus, making it a beautiful target to image. You can see one such photograph below this text, taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. Unfortunately, if $\eta$Car continues on its path of increasing magnitude, its brightness will completely outshine the nebula. From extinction calculations, this will happen when $\eta$Car reaches apparent magnitude somewhere between 3.34 and 2.44, making it about 10 times brighter than the nebula. According to your data analysis in c), give the earliest and latest year during which this can happen.

(Photograph caption: Homunculus Nebula; credits: NASA)

problems.problem: (4 points) The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) can detect gravitational waves from two coalescing black holes. By making extremely accurate measurements at two different locations, it is determined that two black holes were orbiting each other 250 times per second at the instance when their event horizons touched each other. What is the mass of the resulting, larger black hole that formed as a result of the collision? For this calculation you can assume that the black holes had zero spin and you can neglect the loss of black hole mass converted to energy of the gravitational waves.
